thread.title: After the Bell: Oops, Tech Did It Again

author: Ben Levisohn
title: After the Bell: Oops, Tech Did It Again
text:
By Ben Levisohn July 30, 2018 5:21 p.m. ET Everybody Hurts. The Dow Jones Industrial Average succumbed to extreme tech weakness Monday, as investors continued to sell Twitter and Facebook. The Bank of Japan's meeting, and Apple's earnings, due after Tuesday's close, will have a chance to stop the bleeding...or make it worse. In today's After the Bell , we...
•...wonder if the S&P 500 is setting up for a drop;
•...explain why Twitter sunk to the bottom of the S&P 500;
•...and review earnings from Franklin Resources (BEN), which was the S&P 500's best-performing stock.
Stocks... Investors have been wondering if the market can keep rising even if technology is tumbling . For one day, at least, the answer was no.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.4% to 7630, and has now dropped 3.8% over the past three trading days, the largest such decline since March 23. And while the Nasdaq suffered the most, other major indexes didn't escape unscathed. The S&P 500 fell 0.6% to 2802.60, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 144.23 points, or 0.6%, to 25,306.83. It was the blue-chip benchmark's largest decline since July 11.
The S&P 500 is still on track for a good month--it's up 3.1% in July--but there's an ominous pattern forming in its chart. The S&P 500 has gained for four straight weeks, and is within spitting distance of its Jan. 26 high. That, coincidentally, was the last time the S&P 500 rose for four straight weeks, and marked the beginning of the market's correction. Now, Instinet's Frank Cappelleri sees sighs of a potential bearish head-and-shoulders pattern forming in the index:
"While the formation is relatively small, if it’s completed, the most recent push above 2,800 could be history," Cappelleri explains.
So what would the S&P 500 need to begin a slide lower? Apple is (AAPL) set to release earnings after tomorrow's close , and a miss there could send the entire market sliding. Remember, it's the only FAANG stock in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Then there's the meeting of the Bank of Japan , which could decide to let longer-term rates rise as a way of increasing net interest margins for Japanese lenders. Just the mention of higher yields in Japan has caused tremors in the market, and the reality could have an even larger impact.
See you tomorrow.
The Hot Stock Franklin Resources (BEN) shot to the top of the S&P 500 today after the firm's earnings beat Wall Street expectations.
The asset-management firm was up $1.86, or 5.7%, to $34.41.
Christopher Harris, analyst with Wells Fargo, wrote that despite the upside in EPS in Franklin's third quarter, the company posted moderately disappointing revenue, operating income and fund flows, lowering its guidance for the fourth quarter. “We continue to expect negligible revenue and earnings growth and on the lower earnings expectations, our price target decreases modestly from $35 to $34,” said Harris
The shares have lost 20.8% year to date and 23.2% for the past year.

— Varada Bhat
The Biggest Loser Twitter (TWTR) stock continued to fall on Monday on the heels of a drop in monthly active users and disappointing growth.
The microblogging company lost $2.74, or 8.7%, to $31.38.
The company on Friday announced muted user growth and lowered its outlook for margins for the third quarter. “While investing aggressively to clean up the platform and adjust to the new regulatory realities should rightfully be management's top priority at this point, we think timing for when these investments start abating and to show signs for improvement in user growth will remain elusive for some time,” wrote Youssef Squali, analyst at SunTrust Robinson Humphrey. He lowered the price target to $30 from $33.
Despite the drop, shares of Twitter are up 30.7% year to date.
